bottleneck: Guide RNA design tools predict on-target activity and likely off-target sites from sequence, but they miss critical context: chromatin accessibility, epigenetic marks, cell-type-specific repair pathways, and dosage effects all shift real editing outcomes away from predictions. Computational models trained on one cell type transfer poorly to another, and experimental conditions like delivery method further confound results. Predictions therefore disagree with measured edits often enough that every therapeutic guide still requires expensive empirical validation.
current_state: Machine-learning predictors keep improving, yet regulators and developers treat them as screening tools, not substitutes for cell- and tissue-specific off-target assays. Validation remains mandatory and slow.

sources.title: The off-target problem the gene editing industry can no longer afford to ignore

title: Guide RNA prediction gaps force empirical validation
why_it_blocks: If every guide must be validated in the relevant cells and tissues, development stays slow and costly, with each new target repeating the same expensive assays. Closing the prediction gap would compress timelines from years to months for each new therapeutic target.
